webpage.text:
Crisis Management – It’s all in the rhythm

Kevin O'Leary


Kevin O'Leary

Published Dec 24, 2016

My time in the police command team for the London 2012 Olympic and Paralympic games was a rich and valuable experience I’ll always cherish. It seemed as though everyone joined in the spirit of the games and an indicator for me was that strangers actually spoke to each other on public transport! A far cry from the usual vow of silence most commuters observed before and after this period.


I had responsibility for a team of detectives, forensic examiners, intelligence officers and support staff who did an amazing job, none more so than when I and other senior officers got out of their way to let them get on with doing what they do every day to prevent and detect crime in London. 

The strategy was clear in that we weren’t to view the games as a security operation, but reflect the look and feel of the world’s greatest sporting event in our approach to policing the games. We were to provide a security presence in keeping with the Olympic culture and spirit and like any other major operation, information was key to successfully keeping on top of everything we had to do to protect the games and manage London’s busiest summer. 

> To deliver a safe and secure Games, in keeping with the Olympic culture and spirit.

2012 Olympic and Paralympic Safety and Security Strategy (Home Office, 2011)

Although we weren’t operating in crisis mode, we adopted ways of working that I recognise as good practice for crisis management; especially in the way we managed information and maintained situational awareness across all of the teams. The ‘operating rhythm’ was a structure for meetings, briefings and the exchange of information that gave us vision when there was volatility, brought understanding when there was uncertainty, provided clarity in complexity and awareness in ambiguity.

The command team would convene in our vast subterranean special operations room, in person or virtually, at the start and end of each day to share updates about incidents that had occurred, along with information and intelligence about what might happen in the next few hours and beyond, so that we could position our resources and capability where it would be most effective.

The day would be punctuated by smaller, quick fire updates every two hours and any emerging incident would be reported by exception to the silver commander and, in turn, to those commanders who could leverage support from their assets to address it.


The benefits of this structure may be readily apparent, though I think it’s worth highlighting some of them below:

 * Everyone knew when the briefings would take place and so would spend a proportionate amount of time in preparation, distilling their information into a concise, pithy, timely and relevant update. This kept the meetings focused and relatively short.
 * Everyone knew what information to bring to meetings and, more importantly, what didn’t need to be reported and discussed ad nauseam.
 * Between meetings and briefings we could get on with our work, putting into effect the strategy and tactics for protecting the games. We weren’t required to do the job ‘by committee’, continuously staying together as a command team.
 * We got to know each other’s problems and challenges, so we were able to share perspectives and ideas whether it was within our direct area of responsibility or not.
 * We were able to challenge information where we had a different source or channel that offered another perspective. By suspending ego and not thinking of our intelligence as the best and only source prevented us from following a number of false leads and saved our resources from being unnecessarily diverted.
 * In essence, the operating rhythm of meetings and briefings gave us confidence to know that things were under control and that we could pivot to face any emerging situation quickly and effectively.

In my crisis management exercises and training, I advise the crisis management team (CMT) to adopt an operating rhythm so that team members can leverage the capability within the organization and communicate with stakeholders, just as we did during 2012. 

There is temptation and comfort for the CMT to stay ‘in committee’ addressing everything together, but there are a number of disadvantages in this, not least the ability to address only one thing at a time. By allowing people to leave the table and give direction to others the response becomes more effective as people are able to accomplish many parallel tasks to address the crisis.  Assembling the CMT together at set times provides the opportunity for exchanging information and developing situational awareness.

In the 30th year of my police career, I learned so much from my role during 2012. It was the biggest non-crisis, crisis management team and situation I’ve ever been involved in. It was a privilege to be part of it and to use that experience in my new career helping leaders to prepare for what might happen and giving them the tools to use their own know-how effectively to confront the worst case scenarios that come with operating in a volatile business world.

Kevin O’Leary is a Director of Risk Angels Ltd (riskangels.com), a UK based risk and crisis management advisory and training provider. He was a hostage and crisis negotiator at Scotland Yard and the crime and intelligence commander for the London 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. He has a master’s degree in risk, crisis and disaster management from the University of Leicester and is a Fellow of the Chartered Management Institute.

  Replacing the union flags hung for the Queen's Diamond Jubilee, the 156 nations who are heading to London to represent their countries in the Olympics are represented in one of the capital's busiest streets.
  
  Ten thousand athletes are expected to compete in the Games; imagine Regent Street on a busy Saturday, only with super fit people replacing the bargain-hunting shoppers.

  Also, seriously. Did they commission a kid to draw South Korea's?
